scenario.name: Employee monitoring
scenario.idea: Software that scores remote employees' productivity from keystrokes and screenshots and flags low performers.

advisor.summary: This product continuously monitors remote workers and scores them, so it carries high risk in all four categories, mainly because it handles intrusive data and its output can affect people's jobs. Several issues, including EU AI Act classification, monitoring of candidates, and California coverage, depend on facts not yet given and need legal review before launch.

risks.severityWhy: High: continuous, intrusive monitoring of people's data with no safeguards described, which could block launch in the EU/UK.
risks.title: Continuous keystroke and screenshot capture without a clear lawful basis or minimisation
risks.why: Capturing every keystroke and periodic screenshots of employees (and possibly candidates) is broad, hard to justify as necessary, and employees may not be able to freely consent. Data protection rules on lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimisation, and retention may apply in the EU/UK. California privacy rules may also apply to employee data.
risks.fix: Collect activity metadata (active time, app category) instead of raw keystrokes and screenshots. Drop key content entirely. Set short retention with auto-deletion. Add a documented purpose and a lawful-basis assessment per region. Show employees a clear in-app notice of what is collected.

risks.severityWhy: High: sensitive data likely captured incidentally and affects people directly.
risks.title: Screenshots will incidentally capture sensitive and third-party data
risks.why: Screenshots can show health information, union or political messages, private chats, banking pages, passwords, and other people's data. Special-category data rules may apply even if you never intended to collect it.
risks.fix: Add on-device blurring or redaction of non-work apps and windows, an allowlist of monitored apps, automatic pause outside work hours and on personal sites, and a user-visible pause control. Never send raw screenshots to the scoring model; extract only minimal features locally and discard the image.

risks.severityWhy: High: systematic monitoring of people with no safeguard described could block EU/UK launch.
risks.title: No impact assessment for systematic employee monitoring
risks.why: Large-scale, systematic monitoring of workers is the kind of processing that may call for a data protection impact assessment in the EU/UK. The founder has not described one.
risks.fix: Complete and keep a written impact assessment before launch covering necessity, less-intrusive alternatives, risks to employees, and mitigations. Make it available to customers (employers) as part of onboarding.

risks.severityWhy: High: the output informs decisions about people (flagging low performers) with direct employment consequences.
risks.title: Low-performer flags may drive unfair or automated-in-practice decisions
risks.why: A human is nominally in the loop, but managers may rubber-stamp scores. Keystroke volume is a poor proxy for output and may penalise people with disabilities, neurodivergent people, carers with irregular hours, non-native typists, and roles that involve thinking, calls, or meetings. Rules on automated decisions with significant effects (EU/UK) and automated decision-making (California) may apply.
risks.fix: Present scores only as one input, never as a ranked list or auto-flag. Require a reviewer to record independent reasons before any adverse action. Show employees their own data and score, offer a way to contest it, and give plain-language explanations of what drove a flag. Block use for hiring, firing, or pay decisions by default.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: a plausible disparate-impact problem that needs testing and monitoring before scaling.
risks.title: No bias or validity testing of the fine-tuned model
risks.why: A fine-tuned model trained on activity data may encode role, device, language, or accessibility differences as 'low productivity'. No testing or monitoring plan has been described.
risks.fix: Test score distributions across role, region, tenure, and accommodation status (where lawfully collectable). Validate scores against real work outcomes. Set a threshold for pausing flags if gaps appear. Log model versions and set up periodic re-testing and an incident process.

risks.severityWhy: High: employment-related AI may be classed as high-risk for EU users, and some features could be restricted, which could block EU launch.
risks.title: EU AI Act classification of worker monitoring and evaluation
risks.why: AI used to monitor or evaluate workers, or to assess candidates, may be on the high-risk list. If the scoring infers emotions or similar traits, a banned-practice check may also matter. Which applies depends on the exact features.
risks.fix: Map each feature (scoring, flagging, any inference of mood, attention, or engagement) against the EU AI Act categories. Remove any inference of emotion or personality. Do not offer the product in the EU until classification is confirmed. Decide whether candidate monitoring is in scope or should be excluded.

risks.severityWhy: High: sensitive data (potential credentials and private content) stored with no safeguards described.
risks.title: Stored keystrokes and screenshots are a high-value breach target
risks.why: Keystroke logs can contain passwords and secrets, and screenshots can contain confidential company and personal data. A breach would directly harm employees. Security and breach-reporting expectations may apply in the EU/UK, and the fine-tuned model could also leak training data.
risks.fix: Encrypt data in transit and at rest with per-customer keys. Strictly limit staff and customer-admin access with audit logs. Never log raw key content. Keep employee data out of model training unless de-identified. Write and test a breach response plan covering EU/UK and California notice duties.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: plausibly applies and needs mitigation before scaling; depends on marketing claims not yet provided.
risks.title: Overstated productivity-accuracy claims and weak employee disclosure
risks.why: Marketing a keystroke score as an objective measure of productivity could be seen as misleading, and covert or poorly disclosed monitoring may raise unfairness concerns. Documentation of intended use and accountability is also unclear.
risks.fix: Limit claims to what you have validated and publish the model's limits. Require customers to give employees clear notice before activating monitoring, and make the product refuse to run in stealth mode. Keep a record of intended use, affected groups, known harms, and who is accountable.

askLawyer: Can we lawfully offer keystroke and screenshot scoring to employers in the EU/UK and California, and what notice, consultation, or consent steps apply to employees versus job candidates?
Would our scoring and flagging feature be treated as high-risk or restricted under EU AI Act rules, and does it trigger automated decision-making rules in California or the EU/UK?
Who is the controller or processor between us and our employer customers, and what contract terms should allocate responsibility for monitoring, retention, and employee rights requests?

plain.text:
# Risk assessment: AI productivity scoring from keystrokes and screenshots

**Overall:** This is a high-risk concept, legally, technically, and commercially. The biggest problems are that the inputs are weak proxies for productivity, and that the monitoring is highly invasive in exactly the jurisdictions you're targeting.

## 1. Legal and regulatory (highest severity)

**EU/UK**
- **EU AI Act:** AI that monitors and evaluates worker performance or behavior, or informs decisions on termination, promotion, or task allocation, is **high-risk** (Annex III, employment). That means risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, transparency to workers, and conformity assessment. If the system infers emotions or engagement states, it risks falling under the **workplace emotion-recognition prohibition**, which carries the top penalty tier.
- **GDPR/UK GDPR:**
  - You need a lawful basis. Consent is generally invalid in employment because of the power imbalance, and legitimate interest must pass a strict necessity and proportionality test. Continuous keystroke and screenshot capture often fails it. EU regulators have fined companies for similar monitoring.
  - A **DPIA** is effectively mandatory.
  - **Article 22** limits solely automated decisions with significant effects. A "human in the loop" who rubber-stamps flags may not count as meaningful human involvement.
  - Data minimization, purpose limitation, transparency, and access and objection rights all apply.
  - Keystroke dynamics can become biometric data if used for identification.
- **Works councils and labor law:** Germany, France, the Netherlands, and others require consultation or co-determination before deploying monitoring tools. Some countries restrict covert or continuous monitoring outright.

**California**
- **CCPA/CPRA** covers employee and applicant data: notice at collection, access, deletion, and limits on sensitive data. The CPPA's automated decision-making technology rules add notice, opt-out or appeal, and risk-assessment duties.
- **FEHA automated-decision regulations** (effective late 2025) make employers and their vendors liable for discriminatory impact from automated tools.
- **Privacy and wiretap law:** The California constitutional right to privacy and CIPA (Penal Code §631/632) create exposure, especially if screenshots capture personal communications or off-duty activity on personal devices.
- **Labor law:** Monitoring of protected concerted activity (for example, employees discussing pay or organizing) can violate the NLRA. Pending California workplace-surveillance and AI bills could change requirements quickly.

**Candidates:** Using this on applicants (for example, during take-home tests) raises the same problems, plus pre-employment discrimination, disability-accommodation, and transparency issues. I'd treat this as a separate product and likely exclude it.

## 2. Validity and fairness

- **Keystrokes and screenshots are poor proxies for productivity.** They measure activity, not output or quality. Thinking, meetings, calls, whiteboarding, code review, and reading all look "unproductive."
- **Role bias:** Scores will be systematically skewed across roles, such as writers vs. designers vs. managers vs. engineers.
- **Disparate impact:**
  - Employees with motor disabilities, RSI, or dyslexia, and those using dictation or assistive tech, may score low.
  - Neurodivergent workers, older workers, caregivers with fragmented schedules, and non-native speakers (typing speed, language) may also be penalized.
  - Disability discrimination (ADA, FEHA, UK Equality Act) is a serious exposure, and you have no obvious ground-truth labels to audit against.
- **Label problem:** If you fine-tune on manager ratings, you encode managers' biases. If you fine-tune on activity metrics, you're just automating the proxy.
- **Gaming and Goodhart's law:** Mouse jigglers, fake typing, and busywork will defeat the score, and honest workers will be disadvantaged relative to those who game it.
- **Drift and context:** Changes in tools, workflows, or team structure will silently degrade the model.

## 3. Privacy and security

- **Screenshots capture far more than work:** passwords, health information, banking, personal messages, children's data, privileged legal or medical content, and third-party and customer data. That makes you a processor of highly sensitive data you didn't intend to collect.
- **Breach impact:** A central store of employee screenshots and activity logs is a high-value target. A breach could be catastrophic and trigger GDPR/CCPA notification and liability.
- **Cross-border transfers:** EU/UK data processed or stored in the US requires transfer mechanisms (SCCs, the UK addendum, the DPF).
- **Retention creep:** Screenshots tend to be kept indefinitely "just in case."
- **Insider misuse:** Managers could use the data for stalking, retaliation, or union-busting.

## 4. Human oversight is weaker than it appears

- **Automation bias:** Managers tend to trust a numeric score, especially a "low performer" flag. The human becomes a rubber stamp.
- **Self-fulfilling flags:** A flagged employee gets scrutiny, which produces more evidence of problems.
- **No recourse:** Without explanations, a way to contest scores, and the ability to correct context, you have a fairness problem and a legal one.

## 5. Model and technical risks

- **Open model provenance:** Check licenses (some restrict use cases), training-data provenance, and whether you can document the model well enough for AI Act technical documentation.
- **Explainability:** A fine-tuned LLM or similar model makes it hard to explain why a person was flagged, which GDPR and AI Act transparency require.
- **Multimodal screenshot analysis** is error-prone. It misreads context, and it can leak data into logs, prompts, or training sets.
- **Training on employee data** raises its own purpose-limitation and consent problems.

## 6. Business and reputational

- **Trust and attrition:** Surveillance tends to reduce morale, trust, and retention, and can lower real productivity. Your customers' best people may leave first.
- **Sales friction:** Enterprise buyers in the EU will face works councils, DPIAs, and procurement questions. Many will decline.
- **Reputation:** Employee-monitoring products attract negative press, activist attention, and regulatory scrutiny.
- **Liability allocation:** As provider, you may share liability with customers as a "provider" of a high-risk AI system.

## 7. Ways to reduce risk (or pivot)

1. **Change the signal.** Measure outcomes (deliverables, cycle time, goals) rather than keystrokes and screenshots. This is more valid and far less invasive.
2. **Drop screenshots**, or use on-device processing with automatic redaction and short retention. Avoid central storage of raw captures.
3. **Aggregate and team-level insights** (workload, bottlenecks, burnout risk) instead of individual low-performer flags.
4. **Don't use it on candidates.**
5. **Governance by design:**
   - A DPIA and AI Act conformity plan from the start.
   - Works-council
